reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Characterised by painful, progressive global restriction of shoulder movement with the hallmark loss of passive external rotation, distinguishing it from rotator cuff disease
The condition typically evolves through overlapping phases: a painful freezing phase, a stiff frozen phase, and a gradual thawing phase of recovery
It most often affects middle-aged patients and is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, which also predicts a more resistant course
May be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to trauma, immobilisation, or shoulder surgery
Diagnosis is clinical; radiographs are typically normal and mainly serve to exclude other causes such as arthritis or a locked posterior dislocation
Management is largely supportive: analgesia, maintaining movement, physiotherapy, and reassurance about eventual improvement
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection can help pain and stiffness, particularly in the early painful phase
Refractory cases may be treated with capsular hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia, or arthroscopic capsular release
reference.pathophysiology: Frozen shoulder involves inflammation and progressive fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint capsule, particularly the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament. Fibroblastic proliferation and contracture thicken and tighten the capsule, reducing the intra-articular volume and mechanically limiting movement, with external rotation lost first and most severely. The initial inflammatory, hypervascular stage is painful; as the capsule matures into dense fibrous tissue the pain lessens but stiffness dominates; finally the capsule gradually remodels and mobility returns. The strong association with diabetes and certain endocrine and metabolic states points to a systemic predisposition to abnormal fibrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Referred pain from the cervical spine
Septic arthritis (if acute, hot, and systemically unwell)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment demonstrating global restriction with markedly reduced passive external rotation
Plain shoulder radiographs to exclude arthritis, dislocation, or bony lesions
Blood glucose or HbA1c given the association with diabetes
MRI or ultrasound if a rotator cuff tear or other structural lesion is suspected
Thyroid function tests where clinically indicated
redFlags: Constitutional symptoms or a mass suggesting tumour rather than capsulitis
Hot, swollen, systemically unwell shoulder raising concern for septic arthritis
History of significant trauma with fixed internal rotation suggesting a missed posterior dislocation
Rapidly progressive neurological symptoms pointing to an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Frozen shoulder is usually self-limiting, with most patients recovering good function over one to three years, though some, particularly those with diabetes, are left with residual stiffness; interventions can shorten symptoms and relieve pain but recovery is generally slow.
pitfalls: Confusing it with a rotator cuff tear by not testing passive external rotation
Forcing painful manipulation during the acute inflammatory phase, worsening symptoms
Missing an underlying posterior dislocation or arthritis by omitting radiographs
Overlooking undiagnosed diabetes in a patient presenting with adhesive capsulitis
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Analgesia with paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to control pain during the inflammatory freezing phase
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection to reduce capsular inflammation and pain, most useful in the early painful stage
Physiotherapy with supervised stretching and range-of-motion exercises, targeting recovery of the lost external rotation
Hydrodilatation (arthrographic capsular distension) as an option for persistent stiffness
Optimise glycaemic control in diabetic patients, who tend to follow a more resistant course
Reserve manipulation under anaesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release for refractory, disabling disease
Reassure regarding the generally self-limiting course while monitoring functional recovery
